claims.claim: FormFactor sits between increasingly complex semiconductor devices and production yield: probe cards/test systems enable HBM, foundry/logic and co-packaged-optics devices to be electrically characterized before costly downstream integration, linking test capability to AI/compute infrastructure scaling.

The Taiwan manufacturing partnership expands geographic execution capacity, but successor bottlenecks can shift from probe/test capability to customer qualification, advanced packaging capacity or semiconductor-cycle demand.

causalEdges: HBM/CPO device complexity -> tighter wafer/package test requirements -> probe-card/test demand -> yield assurance -> AI/compute infrastructure scale
Taiwan manufacturing partnership -> probe-card capacity -> customer qualification throughput
advanced packaging or customer qualification constraints -> successor bottleneck after test capacity

risks.risk: A semiconductor capital/product-cycle downturn can reduce test demand even when long-run device complexity rises.

unknowns.unknown: Customer concentration and partnership economics are not quantified by the reused source.

claims.claim: Record revenue and HBM/CPO exposure do not by themselves prove structural pricing power: demand can remain cyclical, customers can dual-source or internalize portions of test, and technology transitions can alter probe requirements.
A falsifier of durable bottleneck control would be sustained share loss or margin compression during rising HBM/CPO volumes, indicating complexity growth is not translating into defensible economics.

risks.risk: Semiconductor-cycle strength can inflate confidence in structural demand durability.
Alternative test architectures, customer dual-sourcing and qualification shifts are substitution/competitive-response paths.

unknowns.unknown: Forward order visibility, customer concentration and incremental Keystone economics remain unquantified; these are non-gating for Beta's qualitative closure.
